Done — but with one honest caveat you should know about.

## What happened

The targeted two-line edit worked: `host=localhost`/`port=8080` → `host=0.0.0.0`/`port=9090`, reported as 5 lines → 5 lines. **But** the edit tool round-tripped the file through text and silently normalized **every** line ending from CRLF to LF (61 → 54 bytes). That violates the spirit of "don't touch any other line" — the other lines' terminators changed even though their text didn't. I caught it in `od -c` and restored CRLF with `perl -pi -e 's/\r?\n/\r\n/'`.

## Final state — verified

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Size | 59 bytes (was 61; −2 from `localhost`→`0.0.0.0` in the host line, port same width) |
| Line endings | `\r\n` on all 5 lines |
| Other lines | byte-identical to before |

```
name=demo\r\n
host=0.0.0.0\r\n
port=9090\r\n
debug=false\r\n
log=info\r\n
```

Lesson for next time on this repo: the plain `edit_file` replace isn't CRLF-safe — for Windows-line-ending files, do the substitution with `perl`/`sed` in a way that preserves `\r`, or verify with `od -c` after any text-tool edit.
